title: Nucleus and Binding Energy
notes: The mass of a nucleus is less than the mass of its protons and neutrons weighed separately. The difference Δm is the mass defect.
Einstein's relation turns that mass into energy: binding energy = Δm c^2. In nuclear units, 1 atomic mass unit corresponds to 931 MeV.
The binding energy is the energy you must supply to separate the nucleus into individual nucleons. It is not an energy the nucleus has sitting as kinetic energy.
Binding energy per nucleon is the binding energy divided by the mass number A. It rises from the light nuclei, peaks near iron, and falls slowly for the heavy nuclei.

Fusion of very light nuclei moves them up the curve and releases energy. Fission of a very heavy nucleus also moves the pieces up the curve and releases energy. Both are movements toward higher binding energy per nucleon.
A calculated binding energy uses the actual masses, not the integer mass number. Using A as if it were the nuclear mass in u is the usual mistake.
confusion: ❌ Thinking nuclear mass equals sum of nucleons ✅ Nuclear mass is less than the sum of its constituents' masses; the difference is the mass defect, converted into binding energy (E = mc²).
❌ Misinterpreting binding energy per nucleon as total binding energy ✅ Binding energy per nucleon determines nuclear stability; higher values generally indicate a more stable nucleus.
❌ Confusing fusion and fission energy release ✅ Both processes release energy, but fusion involves combining light nuclei, while fission involves splitting heavy nuclei.
A larger mass defect means a more tightly bound nucleus, not a heavier one.
Binding energy is the energy to pull the nucleus apart.
Per nucleon, not the total, is what the stability curve plots.
